This is the story I was told when wanting to know why American healthcare costs so much:

The last time American healthcare was the best in cost and service was just before WWII, when the government had no involvement. Franklin Roosevelt needed all those tanks, planes, vehicles, guns and bullets to fight the war, so there was a high demand for labor. Unfortunately, most of the labor was oversees dying and getting shot at. Manufacturers had to increase their prices to get more Big Bettys to work for them.

Franklin, however, didn't want to pay more for the stuff he needed, so he enacted price controls. First sign of government involvement. Now manufacturers could only pay their workers so much. So one of them comes up with the idea: We'll offer our workers free healthcare. It was equatable to a gift card redeemable only at a healthcare institution. It worked. Pretty soon, most manufacturing businesses were doing it. The number of insured Americans went from 20 million to 140 million. Even before the post-war economic boom, the healthcare business had exploded.

But now the war is dying down, and the price controls are going away. The healthcare business is worried that the money flow will slow down. So for the first time, they send lobbyists to Washington to make sure employers had to offer their workers health insurance. At the same time, the American Health Association (AHA) is going to specific states, trying to convince them that it's in everyone's best interest to limit the number of universities which could introduce new physicians into their field. This was done exclusively for profit - to increase the cost of medical school. So not only are they limiting the number of doctors that can be put into the market, they used government to create an artificial need for a service that not everyone wanted or even needed.

What happens? Naturally, the price of health care goes up. It continues to do so for the next 20 years. People complain to the government that they should do something, not realizing it was government that started the problem in the first place. A few ideas are tossed around until 1965, when Social Security, Medicare and Medicade are signed into law. Then the price REALLY starts to climb.

This cycle continues, as Ted Kennedy deliberated with congress during his term to try and fix the problem, he created the HMO Act, which was signed into law by Nixon in 1973. This essentially created quasi government healthcare agencies that were the only approved option for employers to offer their employees. If you weren't an HMO, you got pushed further out of the market. It also severely limited the network of doctors people could choose from. What do you think happened then?

The price went up.
